extracted.intended_audience: readers, students, and editors of English literature (especially readers of Samuel Johnson and periodical essays)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and critical standards for assessing or editing Samuel Johnson's periodical essays (The Adventurer and The Idler), emphasizing moral purpose, style, tone, subject-matter, and authorial authenticity. Useful for literary critics, editors, and students studying 18th‑century periodical writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuation of the Rambler (thematic and moral unity)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Adventurer papers by Johnson 'may be considered as a continuation of the Rambler. The same subjects are discussed; the interests of literature and of literary men, the emptiness of praise and the vanity of human wishes.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors/readers should judge these essays by their continuity with Johnson's earlier moral-philosophical concerns — attention to literature and literary men, criticism of vain praise, and reflection on human wishes. Recognition of recurring themes aids attribution and evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognisable authorial style, manner, and sentiments
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Those who are familiar with Johnson's writings can have little hesitation ... in recognising his style, and manner, and sentiments in those papers which are now published under his name.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attribution and quality judgments may rely on internal stylistic evidence — characteristic diction, moral tone, and argumentative manner. Boswell's and Warton’s external notes are complementary but internal recognition is emphasised.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral purpose: promotion of morality and virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: Johnson's essays are judged by their aim of 'promoting the interests of morality and virtue' and by 'rectify[ing] the heart, to purify the passions, to give ardour to virtue and confidence to truth.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess essays by whether they instruct or admonish readers toward moral improvement rather than merely entertain; moral seriousness and remedial intent are positive qualities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of party-politics and personal invective in ethical discussion
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Works of sterling merit, which deal not in party-politics, nor exemplify their ethical discussions by holding out living characters to censure or contempt, win the applause...'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High-quality periodical essays should avoid partisan polemic and the practice of illustrating ethical points by publicly naming or shaming living persons; disinterested moral argument is preferred.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lofty style for sacred/moral subjects
rubrics_metrics.description: 'In his sublime discussions of the most sacred truths, as no style can be too lofty nor conceptions too grand for such a subject, so has the great master never exerted the powers of his great genius with more signal success.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When treating profound moral or religious topics, elevated diction and grand conceptions are appropriate and desirable; restraint toward 'colloquial' style is not required in such contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pure and exalted morality (no easy or compromised virtue)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Here is no cold doctrine of expediency or dangerous speculations on moral approbation, no easy virtue which can be practised without a struggle... Here is no compromise of personal sensuality, for an endurance of others' frailties.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate moral argument as robust and demanding; essays that advocate easy, expedient, or compromised virtue are criticized. True moral seriousness (often tied to religious conviction) is a mark of quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of humour, irony, and raillery with ethical aim (not to wound feeling)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Even in his humorous papers, he never wounds feeling for the sake of raising a laugh, nor sports with folly, but in the hope of reclaiming the vicious and with the design of warning the young.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Satire and humour are praiseworthy when they correct vice or warn the young; cruelty, gratuitous insult, or laughter at suffering are anti-patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intimate knowledge of town manners and contemporary life
rubrics_metrics.description: 'The same intimate knowledge, of the town and its manners is displayed' (as in the Rambler) and the Idler 'delineated in its diversified pages the manners and characters of the day.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Periodical essays should display accurate observation of contemporary social life; vivid, local detail and character-delineation increase an essay's value and appeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variety of subjects to suit periodical readership
rubrics_metrics.description: 'From the greater variety of its subjects ... the sale of the Adventurer was greater than that of the Rambler on its first appearance.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For success in periodical publication, a range of topics (serious and light, transient and permanent) engages readers; editors should balance variety with coherence of purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone and register matched to occasion: more worldly vs. closet philosophy
rubrics_metrics.description: The Idler 'breathes more of a worldly spirit, and savours less of the closet than Johnson's earlier essays; and, accordingly, we find delineated ... the manners and characters of the day.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessors should expect and accept shifts in tone between publications: some essays are appropriately philosophical and reflective (Rambler), others more social, topical, and playful (Idler). Appropriateness of register to intended medium is a quality metric.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance of study, composition, and conversation in intellectual accomplishment
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Study, composition, and converse equally necessary to intellectual accomplishment' — the Idler and similar work reflect varied sources of thought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good essays often arise from a mix of scholarship, drafting, and social discourse. Evaluate both learned references and the fruits of social observation and conversation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of affectation and sentimental puling in pathos
rubrics_metrics.description: On sorrow: 'Here is no affectation of sentimentality, no morbid and puling complaints, but the dignified and chastened expression of sorrow.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective pathos should be dignified and restrained; sentimentalism, excess, or mawkishness are flaws. Genuine feeling expressed with moderation is preferred.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independence of judgment: not prostituting the pen to fear or favour
rubrics_metrics.description: 'A writer ... who never prostituted his pen to fear or favour; and who, though erroneous often in his estimate of men and measures, still, in his support of a party, firmly believed himself to be the advocate of morality and right.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Integrity and independence of voice are positive criteria even when political or other judgments are debatable; moral conviction that resists patronage is valued.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of learned or recondite authorities when relevant
rubrics_metrics.description: Reference to 'recondite medical writers' in some papers and examples from classical authors (Horace, Virgil) appear in criticism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appropriate erudition and classical learning can strengthen essays; obscure references should be defensible by context and authorial expertise rather than gratuitous obscurity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity versus necessary obscurity (ancient poetry necessarily obscure)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Ancient poetry necessarily obscure. Examples from Horace' and the comment that certain obscurities are inherent in ancient texts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics/editors should distinguish between blameworthy obscurity (careless or pretentious) and the unavoidable difficulty of discussing or citing inherently obscure classical material; contextual explanation may be required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admonish and benefit by varied modes (philosophic reproof or cheerful satire)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'He embraced any opportunity of promoting the interests of morality and virtue ... whether from the chair of philosophic reproof or in the cheerful, social circle.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate an essay's effectiveness by its ability to instruct through multiple tones — solemn moral dissertation and lighter, social satire can both be legitimate means to ethical ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness of topical/political allusion for the medium
rubrics_metrics.description: The Idler 'dwells on the passing incidents of the day ... and abounds with party and political allusion.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When writing for newspapers or weekly periodicals, topical references and political allusion are acceptable and often expected; longevity and universality should be weighed against immediate relevance depending on editorial aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not wound feeling for amusement; aim to reform instead of merely ridicule
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Even in his humorous papers, he never wounds feeling for the sake of raising a laugh ... in the hope of reclaiming the vicious.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Humour and ridicule should be measured and constructive rather than merely contemptuous; reviewers/editors should mark gratuitous cruelty as a defect.
